source: CARDI Rice Pest brochure and beneficial-insects poster (FAO-funded, Plant Protection Program), Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute
text:
Cambodian rice fields host a wide range of natural predators that suppress pest numbers for free, and killing them off with unnecessary spraying often causes secondary pest outbreaks (for example planthoppers resurging after a broad-spectrum insecticide wipes out their natural enemies). Ladybird beetles (មេអង្កាំកយាល) and ground beetles feed on planthopper eggs and nymphs on the stem. Several spider types (wolf spiders, orb-weavers, crab spiders) build webs or ambush pests directly on the rice canopy. Damselflies and dragonflies hunt adult moths and planthoppers above the canopy, and their nymphs living in the paddy water eat mosquito larvae and other aquatic pest larvae. Parasitic wasps lay eggs inside the larvae or pupae of leaf folders and other moths, killing the pest from within. Predatory water bugs and giant water bugs hunt other insect larvae in the flooded paddy water, and frogs and fish living in the flooded field also eat a meaningful number of insect pests.

The practical takeaway for a farmer: preserve field-edge vegetation and standing water habitat where these predators live, and treat insecticide as a last resort rather than routine maintenance, since a healthy predator population is doing continuous pest control at no cost.
